title: Length targets from top-scoring answers
statement: Set a written response's target length from the measured length of top-scoring released answers, not from the size of the answer box.
example: One test's essay box holds about 400 to 460 words, while its top-scoring grade 3 exemplars ran about 130 to 235.
detail: A research report on a state test's grade 3 essay checked a common target of about 400 words against the released scoring guides and found it was the answer box's capacity, 2,300 characters excluding spaces, not the expected length. The top-scoring exemplars it measured across three released years ran about 130 to 235 words, so it set a realistic target of about 150 to 250 words, or 5 to 12 sentences.
against: The counts are approximate and rest on six measured exemplars, two a year over three years of one state's test, and the report marks itself as not the course's own and specific to that state ("Not our course, and Texas-specific.", `grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/extras/alpharead-staar-writing-research.md`, line 12).

evidence.quote: **Word-count QA verdict:** "≈400 words" is the **box CAPACITY, not the expected length**. Box holds **2,300 characters excluding spaces** (≈400–460 words). Top-scoring (3/2) G3 exemplars run **~130–235 words** — typically **150–250 words / 5–12 sentences**. Realistic target ≈ **150–250 words**, not 400.
**Verdict: 400 words is BOX CAPACITY, not target length.**
Box: **2,300 characters, not counting spaces** ≈ **~400–460 words** max capacity — the likely origin of the "400 words" number.
Perfect-trait G3 exemplars run **~130–235 words** (cluster ~180–235). None near 400.
**App recommendation:** set the end-of-unit target at a well-organized **~150–250-word essay**; treat 400 as a ceiling.
